title: 02. Data Structures: Set Comprehension — Basics
summary: A set comprehension creates a new set (unordered, unique elements) using the same comprehension syntax — but with curly braces { } and NO colon (unlike dict comprehension).

sections.title: Explanation — Junior Developer Style
sections.body:
### What is a Set Comprehension?

A **set comprehension** creates a new **set** (unordered, unique elements) using the same comprehension syntax — but with **curly braces `{ }`** and **NO colon** (unlike dict comprehension).

```
{   EXPRESSION   for   VARIABLE   in   ITERABLE  }
  ↑                                               ↑
Curly braces                              Same as list comprehension
(same as dict)                            but NO key: value pair!
```

### Key Properties of Sets

```python
# Sets automatically:
# 1. Remove DUPLICATES
# 2. Are UNORDERED (no index access)
# 3. Support fast membership testing (O(1))

data = [1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 4]
my_set = {x for x in data}
print(my_set)       # {1, 2, 3, 4}  ← duplicates removed!
print(type(my_set)) # <class 'set'>

# How is {x: y} (dict) different from {x} (set)?
d = {x: x**2 for x in range(3)}  # Dict: {0:0, 1:1, 2:4}
s = {x**2 for x in range(3)}     # Set: {0, 1, 4}
```

### When to Use Set Comprehension

```python
# Use when you need:
# 1. Unique values from a collection
# 2. Fast membership testing
# 3. Set operations (union, intersection, difference)

words = ['hello', 'world', 'hello', 'python', 'world', 'hello']

# Get unique words (set comprehension)
unique_words = {w.lower() for w in words}
print(unique_words)  # {'hello', 'world', 'python'}

# Fast: 'hello' in unique_words → O(1)
# Slow: 'hello' in list(words) → O(n)
```

### Example 1: Deduplication

```python
# Primary use case: removing duplicates while transforming

# Duplicate emails from form submissions
emails = [
    'alice@company.com', 'BOB@company.com', 'alice@company.com',
    'carol@company.com', 'bob@company.com', 'ALICE@company.com'
]

# Unique normalized emails
unique_emails = {email.lower().strip() for email in emails}
print(unique_emails)
# {'alice@company.com', 'bob@company.com', 'carol@company.com'}
print(f"Original: {len(emails)}, Unique: {len(unique_emails)}")
# Original: 6, Unique: 3

# Unique first characters
data = ['apple', '
```

```python
data = ['apple', 'avocado', 'banana', 'blueberry', 'cherry', 'apricot', 'cranberry']

# Unique first letters
first_letters = {word[0] for word in data}
print(first_letters)
# {'a', 'b', 'c'}

# Unique word lengths
unique_lengths = {len(word) for word in data}
print(unique_lengths)
# {5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10}  ← all unique lengths present

# Unique domains from emails
mixed_emails = ['alice@gmail.com', 'bob@yahoo.com', 'carol@gmail.com',
                'dave@company.com', 'eve@yahoo.com']
domains = {email.split('@')[1] for email in mixed_emails}
print(domains)
# {'gmail.com', 'yahoo.com', 'company.com'}
```

### Example 2: Unique Values from Complex Data

```python
# Extract unique values from lists of dicts

employees = [
    {'name': 'Alice',  'dept': 'Engineering', 'skill': 'Python'},
    {'name': 'Bob',    'dept': 'Marketing',   'skill': 'Excel'},
    {'name': 'Carol',  'dept': 'Engineering', 'skill': 'Java'},
    {'name': 'Dave',   'dept': 'HR',          'skill': 'Python'},
    {'name': 'Eve',    'dept': 'Engineering', 'skill': 'Python'},
    {'name': 'Frank',  'dept': 'Marketing',   'skill': 'Photoshop'},
]

# All unique departments
departments = {emp['dept'] for emp in employees}
print(departments)
# {'Engineering', 'Marketing', 'HR'}

# All unique skills
skills = {emp['skill'] for emp in employees}
print(skills)
# {'Python', 'Excel', 'Java', 'Photoshop'}

# Unique (dept, skill) combinations
dept_skill_pairs = {(emp['dept'], emp['skill']) for emp in employees}
print(dept_skill_pairs)
# {('Engineering', 'Python'), ('Marketing', 'Excel'),
#  ('Engineering', 'Java'), ('HR', 'Python'), ('Marketing', 'Photoshop')}
```

### Example 3: Set Operations with Comprehensions

```python
# Combine set comprehensions with set operations

team_a_skills = {'Python', 'Django', 'REST API', 'PostgreSQL', 'Docker'}
team_b_skills = {'Python', 'FastAPI', 'REST API', 'MongoDB', 'Kubernetes'}
required_skills = {'Python', 'REST API', 'Docker', 'Kubernetes', 'AWS'}

# Skills team A has that are required
a_meets_required = team_a_skills & required_skills
print("Team A meets:", a_meets_required)
# {'Python', 'REST API', 'Docker'}

# Skills MISSING from Team A
a_missing = required_skills - team_a_skills
print("Team A missing:", a_missing)
# {'Kubernetes', 'AWS'}

# All unique skills across both teams
all_skills = team_a_skills | team_b_skills
print("Combined skills:", all_skills)
# {'Python', 'Django', 'REST API', 'PostgreSQL', 'Docker',
#  'FastAPI', 'MongoDB', 'Kubernetes'}

# Skills only team A has (not team B)
only_a = team_a_skills - team_b_skills
print("Only in Team A:", only_a)
# {'Django', 'PostgreSQL', 'Docker'}
```

### Example 4: Characters and Text Analysis

```python
# Text analysis using set comprehensions

text = "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog"

# Unique characters (excluding spaces)
unique_chars = {c.lower() for c in text if c != ' '}
print(f"Unique chars: {sorted(unique_chars)}")
# All 26 letters — this is a pangram!
print(f"Is pangram: {len(unique_chars) == 26}")
# True

# Unique vowels used
vowels = {c for c in text.lower() if c in 'aeiou'}
print(f"Vowels used: {vowels}")
# {'a', 'e', 'i', 'o', 'u'}

# Unique word lengths
words = text.split()
word_lengths = {len(w) for w in words}
print(f"Unique word lengths: {sorted(word_lengths)}")
# [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]  (wait: 'The'=3, 'quick'=5, 'brown'=5, etc.)

# Unique words (case-insensitive)
unique_words = {w.lower() for w in words}
print(f"Unique words: {len(unique_words)}")

# Check if two texts share common words
text1 = "python is a great programming language"
text2 = "python and java are popular programming tools"
words1 = {w for w in text1.split()}
words2 = {w for w in text2.split()}
common = words1 & words2
print(f"Common words: {common}")
# {'python', 'programming'}
```

### Example 5: Validation and Membership Testing

```python
# Fast membership testing — O(1) with sets!

# Valid choices (use set for fast lookup)
VALID_CURRENCIES = {
    'USD', 'EUR', 'GBP', 'JPY', 'AUD', 'CAD', 'CHF',
    'CNY', 'INR', 'BRL', 'MXN', 'KRW', 'SGD', 'HKD'
}

VALID_STATUSES = {'pending', 'processing', 'completed', 'cancelled', 'refunded'}

BLOCKED_EMAILS = {'spam@test.com', 'fake@example.com', 'blocked@domain.com'}

# Simulated incoming requests
requests = [
    {'currency': 'USD', 'status': 'completed',  'email': 'alice@co.com'},
    {'currency': 'XYZ', 'status': 'pending',    'email': 'bob@co.com'},
    {'currency': 'EUR', 'status': 'unknown',    'email': 'carol@co.com'},
    {'currency': 'GBP', 'status': 'processing', 'email': 'spam@test.com'},
    {'currency': 'INR', 'status': 'completed',  'email': 'dave@co.com'},
]

# Filter valid requests using set membership (O(1) per check!)
valid_requests = [
    req for req in requests
    if req['currency'] in VALID_CURRENCIES      # O(1)
    and req['status']   in VALID_STATUSES       # O(1)
    and req['email']    not in BLOCKED_EMAILS   # O(1)
]

print(f"Valid requests: {len(valid_requests)}/{len(requests)}")
for r in valid_requests:
    print(f"  ✅ {r}")

# Find unique invalid currencies in the batch
invalid_currencies = {
    req['currency'] for req in requests
    if req['currency'] not in VALID_CURRENCIES
}
print(f"Invalid currencies found: {invalid_currencies}")
# {'XYZ'}
```
